digest.top_line: POSEIDON: adding HT to PORT missed OS across 6 RCTs (HR 0.87, p=0.06); OS benefit confined to pre-PORT PSA >0.5 ng/mL (HR 0.72 at 0.51-1.00, 0.69 >1.00).
digest.tldr: Prostate carried the day. POSEIDON limits HT with PORT to pre-PORT PSA >0.5. GÖTEBORG-1 shows 25-yr PCSS 94% on AS, but only 38% of men were still treatment-free at 22 yr. The RT dose and planning signals are hypothesis-generating: retrospective SIB escalation in MIBC TMT, and a preprint randomized phase II of immune-sparing lung SBRT.

sites.intro: First international IROCK consensus on iGTV delineation for localized RCC SABR.

studies.name: IROCK RCC SABR contouring guidelines
studies.tldr: First international consensus on target delineation for localized RCC SABR: 16 experts, median DSC 0.85 vs consensus, >0.70 in every case.
details: 🔍 16 IROCK radiation oncologists, each with ≥10 RCC SABR cases; US, Canada, Australia, Netherlands, India
🔍 4 CT-only cases contoured on EduCase; STAPLE 95% consensus contour, then 2 consensus meetings

details.text: 🧭 Consensus target statements by scenario

rows: Tumor >10 cm with IVC tumor thrombus
Primary tumor + entire tumor thrombus; exclude bland thrombus
All visible tumor, account for internal motion; may extend into hilum
All visible gross tumor; surgical clips need not be included
Visible gross recurrence + entire ablation cavity

details.text: 📊 Participant vs consensus contour agreement, median (IQR)
🧭 All-case planning statements
subdetails: OAR constraints prioritized over target coverage; heterogeneous coverage with steep gradient
Dose hotspot placed within the iGTV
No microscopic-spread margin; most common PTV margin 5 mm uniform on iGTV
Contrast CT or MRI; nephrology referral if contrast nephrotoxicity risk

details: 🧭 Renal cortex = ipsilateral kidney minus iGTV, renal pelvis, vasculature, proximal ureter
🧭 Renal hilum optional, not a dose-limiting OAR; no evidence it reduces renal artery stenosis
📐 2-way ANOVA: DSC/MDA/HD differed by case (P < .05); MDA also differed by participant (P = .03)
⚠️ CT-only images; no recontouring after consensus meetings to confirm reduced variation
⚠️ Table 2 fraction-specific OAR constraints (FASTRACK-II / AQuOS-II derived) not attributable row-wise from source text

verdict.rationale: Expert contouring consensus; agreement metrics measure contour overlap, not outcome. Standardizes target definition for an emerging indication; not validated prospectively.
verdict.audience: Localized RCC treated with SABR, incl. IVC thrombus, recurrence, post-RFA

studies.significance: The two contested target calls are settled: include the entire tumor thrombus and the entire RFA cavity, and these were also the cases with most variation (DSC 0.85 and 0.75; HD 64.60 mm in Case 1). The 5 mm PTV assumes 4DCT, vacuum cushion, IV contrast and daily CBCT, so a center without those shouldn't copy the margin.
studies.monday_clinic: In a medically inoperable localized RCC with IVC tumor thrombus or recurrence after RFA, this supports covering the full thrombus or full ablation cavity in the iGTV; it does not settle the dose or fraction number, which the panel left institution-specific.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Contouring consensus: **16** IROCK radiation oncologists contoured **4 CT-only cases**; a STAPLE algorithm produced the 95% consensus contour, refined over **2 online meetings** (May and June 2024) until **100% agreement** on statements.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Panel eligibility: **≥10 RCC SABR cases treated**; 14 of 16 had treated ≥10 pts in the prior 12 months. Cases: >10 cm tumor with IVC thrombus, central tumor at the hilum, post-nephrectomy recurrence, post-RFA residual.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: iGTV equals ITV since **no microscopic-spread margin** is added. Most common PTV: **uniform 5 mm** on iGTV with supine vacuum cushion, 4DCT, IV contrast and daily CBCT. Participants used **1, 3, or 5 fractions**; OAR constraints drawn from FASTRACK-II and AQuOS-II protocols.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Overall **median DSC 0.85** (range 0.40-0.95), MDA **2.17 mm**, HD **9.00 mm**; median DSC >0.70 in every case. Greatest variation in Case 1 (superior thrombus extent) and Case 4 (cavity inclusion).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: FASTRACK-II established prospective phase II support for RCC SABR; this document standardizes the target and OAR definitions that trial-era protocols left variable. AQuOS-II is prospectively testing whether ipsilateral parenchyma and hilum contours matter for toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localized RCC treated with SABR in centers with 4DCT, contrast and CBCT. Does not represent MRI-guided or adaptive workflows, where the 5 mm margin may differ.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **CT-only** images; MRI might have reduced variation. Participants did **not recontour** after consensus, so the post-consensus agreement is assumed rather than measured.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The guideline chooses **OAR priority over coverage** and accepts heterogeneous target dose, which trades some target coverage for bowel safety. Whether hilum or cortex sparing reduces renal toxicity remains **unanswered** and is deliberately left optional.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this paper sits less in its agreement statistics than in the decisions it makes on the scenarios where RCC SABR practice has been most improvised. Tumor thrombus, ablation cavities, post-nephrectomy recurrences near bowel, and central tumors at the hilum are exactly the cases a center starting a kidney SABR program is likely to see, because they are the patients surgeons and interventional radiologists hand off. Before this, a radiation oncologist faced with an IVC thrombus or a failed RFA had protocol documents from trials like FASTRACK-II and AQuOS-II for dose and constraints, but no shared rule for where the target ends.

The agreement metrics should be read carefully. A DSC is overlap with a consensus that was itself built from the same participants' contours through STAPLE weighting, so high agreement is partly circular. The more informative numbers are the outliers: Case 1 carried an HD of 64.60 mm and Case 4 a DSC of 0.75, and these are precisely the two cases where the panel had to make a policy decision (how far up the thrombus, how much cavity). In other words, experienced contourers agree on tumor edges; they disagree on intent. The guideline resolves intent by choosing inclusion, the whole thrombus and the whole cavity, on the rationale that an in-cavity recurrence outside the field would be hard to retreat. That is a reasonable judgment, but it is a judgment, and it will enlarge targets in exactly the cases where OARs are hardest to spare.

The panel's answer to that tension is explicit: OAR constraints outrank target coverage, with heterogeneous dose and the hotspot inside the iGTV. This mirrors how SABR is delivered for pancreas and other upper abdominal targets and is probably the most transferable statement in the paper. It also means that reported coverage objectives are aspirational in the difficult cases, which matters for any future trial using these contours as a quality benchmark.

The renal substructure question is handled with appropriate restraint. The panel declined to make the hilum a dose-limiting structure, noting no evidence that sparing it reduces renal artery stenosis or ureteric stricture, and warned that pushing dose away from it may raise dose to functioning parenchyma. That is the right default until AQuOS-II reports.

What would make this wrong? Prospective patterns-of-failure data showing marginal recurrences with the 5 mm PTV, or toxicity signals from the larger thrombus and cavity targets. The margin also rests on a specific workflow (vacuum immobilization, 4DCT, contrast, daily CBCT); centers without that chain should not import the number unchanged. The guideline defines geometry, not dose, and the fractionation question remains institution-specific.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The two contested target calls are settled: include the entire tumor thrombus and the entire RFA cavity, the cases with most variation (DSC 0.85 and 0.75). The 5 mm PTV assumes 4DCT, vacuum cushion, IV contrast and daily CBCT, so it does not transfer unchanged to other workflows.

open_questions: Does renal hilum or cortex sparing reduce renal toxicity?
Patterns of failure with the 5 mm PTV margin
Does MRI-based contouring reduce target variation?

sites.intro: Two long-horizon datasets: which men get HT with salvage RT, gated by pre-PORT PSA, and 25-yr AS outcomes from the pre-MRI era.

studies.name: GÖTEBORG-1 active surveillance, 25-year follow-up
studies.tldr: 25-yr PC-specific survival 94% (CI 91-98%) on AS, but 22-yr failure-free survival 68% and treatment-free survival 38%.
details: 🔍 AS cohort nested in the GÖTEBORG-1 screening trial; AS was not randomized, and choosing it was left to the physician and pt

details.text: 🔍 N=488 screen-detected pts: 251 very-low, 129 low, 108 intermediate risk; high-risk excluded
🔍 Median f/u 18.0 yr (IQR 14.7-22.1) in survivors; median age 66, median PSA 4.1 ng/ml
⚠️ No predefined AS protocol: PSA every 6-12 mo, rebiopsy only on clinical progression

details: ⚠️ Pre-MRI era: sextant biopsies until 2009, only 21 pts had prediagnostic MRI

details.text: 📊 Kaplan-Meier outcomes, whole cohort (TFS/FFS truncated at 22 yr)
📊 Outcomes by risk group (TFS/FFS at 19 yr, PCSS/OS at 24 yr)
💊 Exits from AS: 232 men discontinued
📊 Failure in 81 men, counted by the most severe event
subdetails: PSA relapse after RP/RT, no HT: 18

details.text: 📐 Multivariable Cox model for failure (baseline factors)
subdetails: PSA density per doubling: HR 1.78 (1.22-2.59), p=0.003

details.text: 📊 Nearly half of all failures occurred >10 yr after diagnosis
⚠️ The broad failure definition includes untreated low-PSA relapse after RT (nadir +2) or RP (≥0.2 ng/ml)
🔗 PC mortality in the same range as ProtecT (3.4%) and Toronto (5.7% at 15 yr); lower than PIVOT (11.4%)
🔗 15-yr TFS 48% is in line with Toronto (55%, 15 yr) and PASS (49%, 10 yr)

verdict.rationale: Nonrandomized AS cohort with no comparator arm and no predefined surveillance protocol. Pre-MRI sextant selection limits how far the result transfers to contemporary AS.
verdict.audience: Screen-detected very-low/low/intermediate-risk localized PC on AS

studies.significance: RT was the exit for 44 of 488 men, but the paper reports no outcomes by treatment, so the efficacy of delayed RT after AS can't be separated out. Failure kept accruing past 10 yr in every risk group. For a man choosing AS over upfront RT, the trade is decades of monitoring, not a 10-15 yr window.
studies.monday_clinic: In a screen-detected very-low or low-risk man, this supports AS as low risk for PC death out to 25 yr. In intermediate-risk disease (24-yr PCSS 85%, 19-yr FFS 55%), it supports discussing upfront definitive therapy as a real alternative. It does not extend to high-risk PC.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Observational AS cohort inside the **GÖTEBORG-1 PSA screening trial** (1995 to 2014 diagnoses, follow-up to Dec 31, 2023). Data were collected prospectively, but **AS was not randomized** and followed **no predefined protocol**. Kaplan-Meier estimates plus a multivariable Cox model for failure.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Of 1052 screen-detected PCs, 494 (47%) were on AS and **488 were included**: 251 very-low, 129 low, 108 intermediate risk. High-risk excluded. Median age 66, PSA 4.1 ng/ml, PSA density 0.12.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Treatment-free, **failure-free** (noncurative PSA relapse, starting HT, metastasis, or PC death), PC-specific, and overall survival, all measured from diagnosis.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT was the active treatment for **44 men** leaving AS, against 141 RP. Post-RT relapse was defined as **nadir +2 ng/ml**. No dose, technique, or RT-specific outcome is reported.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **PCSS 94% at 25 yr** against **FFS 68% at 22 yr**; 14 PC deaths and 81 failures. **Gleason score** (HR 3.12) and **PSA density** (HR 1.78) predicted failure.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PC mortality falls in the range of **ProtecT (3.4%)** and the Toronto cohort (5.7% at 15 yr). It is roughly half of **PIVOT (11.4%)** and well below SPCG-4, a gap the authors attribute to screen detection versus clinical diagnosis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents screen-detected very-low, low, and intermediate-risk localized PC followed with PSA and sextant-era biopsies. Does not represent high-risk PC or MRI-selected, MRI-monitored contemporary AS cohorts.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Gleason reclassification after 2005 means some low-risk pts here would be intermediate risk today. Failure lumps PC death with untreated low-level PSA relapse. Risk-group differences in PCSS were **not formally tested**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Failure hazard stayed **roughly constant over time**, and nearly half of failures came >10 yr after diagnosis, so there is no safe point to stop monitoring. Failures in Gleason 6 pts show that some Gleason 6 tumors do progress.

studies.interpretation:
The durable finding here is not the 94% PC-specific survival at 25 years. Earlier AS series at 10 to 15 years already predicted that. The new information is the pace of failure beyond 15 years. Failure-free survival fell from 81% at 15 years to 68% at 22 years, treatment-free survival kept falling, and nearly half of all failures came more than a decade after diagnosis. Cohorts that stopped at 10 or 15 years, including the PASS and PRIAS-type registries the authors cite, could not see this tail. Screen-detected tumors carry long lead times, so the events that matter show up late.

Set against ProtecT, the result fits rather than contradicts. ProtecT found that men randomized to monitoring carried a higher metastasis risk than men treated upfront, with low PC mortality in every arm. GÖTEBORG-1 reports PC mortality in a similar range (ProtecT 3.4%, Toronto 5.7% at 15 years) and a large burden of failure short of death. Both point the same way: surveillance protects against overtreatment at the cost of some missed cure, and that cost only becomes visible with long follow-up. The contrast with PIVOT and SPCG-4 is best read as a population effect, screen-detected versus clinically diagnosed disease, not as evidence that this AS approach was superior.

Methodology should lower a reader's confidence in how well these numbers transfer, and it cuts in two directions. The cohort was selected and followed with PSA and sextant biopsies, almost no MRI, and no fixed rebiopsy schedule. That likely undersampled disease at entry and caught progression late. Modern MRI-based selection and monitoring should reduce both problems, which would make contemporary outcomes look better. Grading drift pushes the other way: some tumors called low risk here would be graded intermediate risk today and treated upfront. Contemporary AS also increasingly includes favorable intermediate-risk disease, where this cohort already showed the worst figures: 19-year FFS 55% and 24-year PCSS 85%. Those intermediate-risk estimates rest on 108 men with wide intervals, and the paper did not formally test the risk-group differences. They inform counseling but should not be read as precise.

The failure definition also needs scrutiny. It combines PC death, metastasis, starting hormonal therapy, and PSA relapse after surgery or RT with no further treatment. The authors defend this as a failure to achieve the curative intent the men enrolled with. That is reasonable for counseling, but it inflates the event count compared with endpoints that change survival. The 18 men with untreated relapse are a different clinical problem from the 14 who died.

For radiation oncologists the paper is mostly context, not RT evidence. Forty-four men went to RT, but outcomes are not broken out by treatment, so this says nothing about whether delayed RT after long surveillance performs as well as upfront RT. What it does settle is the counseling frame for a man weighing surveillance against definitive therapy: the risk of death is low, but monitoring never ends, and exiting to treatment late is common. What would have to be true for this to overstate the risk is exactly what modern selection claims to fix. That claim still lacks 20-year data.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: RT was the exit for 44 of 488 men, with no outcomes reported by treatment, so the efficacy of delayed RT can't be judged from this paper. Failure keeps accruing past 10 yr, which matters when counseling a man choosing between AS and upfront RT.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: RP was the main exit from AS (141 of 232 discontinuations). Gleason score (HR 3.12) and PSA density (HR 1.78) at diagnosis predicted later failure, which helps identify men who might do better with upfront surgery than with prolonged surveillance.

open_questions: Does MRI-based selection and monitoring lower long-term AS failure?
Is there any safe point to stop AS monitoring?
How does intermediate-risk AS perform under modern grading?

studies.name: POSEIDON
studies.tldr: IPD meta-analysis of 6 RCTs: adding HT to PORT did not improve OS (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76–1.01, p=0.06); benefit confined to pre-PORT PSA >0.5 ng/mL.
details: 🔍 IPD meta-analysis (MARCAP), 6 randomised phase 3 trials, 6057 pts, median f/u 9.0y
🔍 Trials: GETUG-AFU 16, NRG/RTOG 0534, RADICALS-HD (two-way + three-way), RTOG 9601
💊 Short-term HT 4–6 mo (mostly GnRH agonist) vs long-term 24 mo; RTOG 9601 used high-dose bicalutamide
📊 1° EP OS: 10y 83.6% PORT alone vs 84.3% PORT+HT; ASCO Post quotes absolute benefit 0.7%

details.text: 📊 HT effect by randomised comparison (HR vs control)
📊 OS effect of adding HT by pre-PORT PSA

details: 📐 Interaction PSA >0.5 vs ≤0.5: p=0.02; four-strata interaction p=0.08
📐 HT duration × effect interaction p=0.17: no evidence long-term beats short-term for OS
📊 Splines: long-term HT OS CI upper bound below 1.0 only at PSA ≥1.6 ng/mL
📐 MFS gain misses ICECaP surrogate threshold (upper CI <0.81) at every pre-PORT PSA for any HT
⚠️ Long-term HT trials had higher pre-PORT PSA (median 0.5 vs 0.3) and more adverse pathology
⚠️ No multiplicity correction; PSA interaction p varies by model (continuous: one-stage 0.19, two-stage 0.04)
⚠️ ASCO Post quotes NNT 125 (PSA ≤0.2) and 25 (PSA >1.0); Lancet paper reports negative NNT and 12
⚠️ Pre-PSMA PET, pre-Decipher enrolment; discussant: applies only to PET-negative BCR

verdict.rationale: Pooled randomised IPD with prespecified OS primary not met, undercutting routine HT with low-PSA PORT. The PSA >0.5 benefit rests on subgroup interaction, not a primary comparison.
verdict.audience: Post-RP prostate cancer receiving PORT, median pre-PORT PSA 0.3 ng/mL

studies.significance: MFS improved (HR 0.79) but never cleared the ICECaP 0.81 surrogate threshold at any pre-PORT PSA, so the bPFS/MFS gains behind GETUG-AFU 16 and RTOG 0534 were not expected to translate to OS. Duration showed no interaction (p=0.17); long-term HT OS benefit on splines appears only at PSA ≥1.6 ng/mL, above most modern early salvage.
studies.monday_clinic: In PET-negative BCR after RP heading to early salvage PORT at PSA ≤0.5 ng/mL, this questions adding HT for survival; above 0.5 ng/mL it supports HT, with no OS evidence favoring 24 over 4–6 mo; it does not extend to PSMA PET-positive nodal disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **IPD meta-analysis** of six randomised phase 3 trials via the MARCAP consortium (PROSPERO CRD42019134376), one-stage Cox stratified by trial. **6057 pts**, median follow-up **9.0y** (IQR 7.2–10.7).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men receiving PORT after radical prostatectomy for recurrent prostate cancer. Median pre-PORT PSA **0.3 ng/mL** in the any-HT and short-term sets, **0.5 ng/mL** in the long-term set. Race and ethnicity data not available.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Short-term HT 4–6 mo** (GETUG-AFU 16, NRG/RTOG 0534, RADICALS-HD two-way and three-way), predominantly GnRH agonist. **Long-term HT 24 mo** (RADICALS three-way, RTOG 9601); RTOG 9601 used high-dose bicalutamide monotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: overall survival.** Secondary: MFS, event-free survival, biochemical recurrence; prespecified interaction tests for pre-PORT PSA and HT duration.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **No OS benefit overall** (HR 0.87, p=0.06) despite MFS gain (HR 0.79, p<0.001). OS benefit limited to **pre-PORT PSA >0.5 ng/mL** (interaction p=0.02), with NNT 22 at 0.51–1.00 and 12 at >1.00 ng/mL.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: GETUG-AFU 16 and RTOG 0534 established HT with salvage RT on biochemical endpoints; per the ASCO Post write-up only RTOG 9601, a late-salvage trial, had shown an OS benefit. POSEIDON pools these trials and finds the OS signal tracks pre-PORT PSA rather than HT duration.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents PET-negative biochemical recurrence after RP treated with PORT, mostly early salvage. Does not represent PSMA PET-positive nodal or metastatic disease, or biomarker-selected (Decipher) decisions.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Duration comparison is confounded: long-term HT trials enrolled higher-PSA, higher-risk pathology. The PSA interaction is **model-dependent** (continuous PSA: one-stage p=0.19, two-stage p=0.04) and no multiplicity correction was applied. RT dose and field detail not reported in source excerpt.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The trial-level MFS gains held but did not clear the ICECaP surrogate threshold, so the historical case for routine HT with low-PSA salvage rests on endpoints that do not predict OS here. **Short-term HT may suffice** where HT is used; NRG GU006 (PAM50, apalutamide) tests biomarker selection.

studies.interpretation:
The central claim here is less that hormone therapy fails with postoperative radiotherapy than that the benefit the field has inferred from biochemical and metastasis endpoints does not carry through to survival for most men now being treated. GETUG-AFU 16 and RTOG 0534 made short-course HT with salvage RT a common default on the strength of biochemical control. POSEIDON pools those trials with RADICALS-HD and RTOG 9601 at the patient level, and the pooled MFS benefit (HR 0.79) is real but falls short of the ICECaP surrogate threshold of 0.81 at every pre-PORT PSA. That is the methodological hinge: the paper is not just reporting a null OS primary, it is arguing, with a prespecified surrogacy framework, that the prior positive endpoints were never expected to become survival gains in this population.

The PSA story deserves more caution than the trade-press headline gives it. The binary split at 0.5 ng/mL produced an interaction p of 0.02, but the four-strata interaction was 0.08, and PSA as a continuous variable was non-significant in the one-stage model (0.19) and significant only in the two-stage model (0.04). No multiplicity correction was applied, and the authors themselves label secondary subgroup findings hypothesis-generating. The direction is biologically coherent, since higher pre-PORT PSA plausibly marks occult disease beyond the RT field where systemic therapy should matter, and it matches the prior suggestion that PSA is predictive for long-term HT benefit. But the threshold itself should be read as a gradient, not a validated cut point.

The duration question is weaker still as a comparison. Long-term HT looked better on OS (HR 0.79, p=0.049) than short-term (HR 0.93), yet the duration interaction was 0.17, and the long-term trials enrolled men with higher PSA and more adverse pathology. Directly randomised prolongation from short to long course in the RADICALS cohorts improved MFS but not OS (HR 0.89). The spline analysis puts any long-term OS benefit at PSA of 1.6 ng/mL or higher, a range rarely seen in contemporary early salvage. The practical read is that when HT is used, 4 to 6 months carries most of what the data support, with 24 months reserved for the high-PSA tail. The RTOG 9601 bicalutamide arm also means part of the long-term signal comes from a regimen few would use now.

The largest threat to transportability is era. These trials enrolled before PSMA PET and genomic classifiers; the discussant restricts the findings to PET-negative biochemical recurrence. A modern man at PSA 0.3 with a negative PSMA scan is probably well represented, and arguably lower risk than the pooled population. A man whose PSA is 0.3 but whose PSMA PET shows pelvic nodes is not represented at all, and the result should not be stretched to him. For the RT decision itself, POSEIDON does not inform field design, dose, or nodal coverage; the source excerpt reports no RT parameters.

What would make it wrong: if pre-PORT PSA is mostly a proxy for disease biology that a classifier captures better, the PSA threshold could misallocate HT in both directions. NRG GU006, testing PAM50 with short-term apalutamide, is the trial positioned to show whether biology beats PSA as the selector.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: For early salvage PORT at pre-PORT PSA ≤0.5 ng/mL, HT added no OS benefit, so RT alone is a defensible default in PET-negative BCR. Above 0.5 ng/mL the OS HR falls to 0.72 to 0.69; long-term HT OS benefit on splines appears only at PSA ≥1.6 ng/mL.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Duration showed no OS interaction (p=0.17) and prolonging short to long course did not improve OS (HR 0.89), so 4–6 mo carries the supported benefit. MFS gains did not clear the ICECaP threshold, weakening MFS as a basis for systemic intensification with PORT.

open_questions: Does PSMA PET staging change which pts benefit from HT with PORT?
Can a genomic classifier outperform pre-PORT PSA for selecting HT?
Does ARSI-based short-term HT change the OS read?

details: 🔍 Multicentre retrospective, 3 centres, March 2015 to May 2025; N=107 consecutive curative-intent MIBC

details.text: 🔍 39 dose-escalated vs 68 standard dose; median f/u 23 mo (range 3-104)
🔍 RT technique
subdetails: Escalation: SIB up to 60Gy/20fx or 70Gy/32fx to primary lesion
Empty-bladder CT sim; daily CBCT; MRI/PET fusion in select pts

📊 Pattern of recurrence by site (n events)

verdict.rationale: Retrospective, non-randomised; escalated cohort selected (all unifocal, less hydronephrosis). Few invasive events (2 vs 16), adjusted for T stage only, so dose cannot be separated from selection.
verdict.audience: MIBC T2-3, M0 (node+ allowed), post-TURBT curative RT ± concurrent chemo

studies.significance: Pattern of failure is the RT read: standard-dose invasive failures sat at the original tumour site (14 within vs 2 outside), and the escalated cohort had 1 invasive failure inside the boost. A 60Gy/20fx or 70Gy/32fx SIB to the primary on daily CBCT carried no G2+ GU/GI cost, which supports testing primary-tumour escalation in TMT.
studies.monday_clinic: In a unifocal MIBC TMT candidate without hydronephrosis, this supports a primary-tumour SIB as a trial-worthy option rather than routine practice; it does not extend to multifocal disease, which the escalated cohort never included.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Multicentre retrospective** cohort from 3 centres, March 2015 to May 2025. N=107: **39 dose-escalated vs 68 standard**. Median follow-up 23 mo (range 3-104).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Curative-intent MIBC** after TURBT, RT with or without concurrent chemo; **node-positive allowed if M0**. Metastatic or palliative-intent pts excluded. 51% received no chemo, mostly for poor PS or comorbidity.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Standard: **55Gy/20fx or 64Gy/32fx** whole bladder. Escalation: **SIB up to 60Gy/20fx or 70Gy/32fx** to the primary lesion. Empty-bladder CT sim, daily CBCT, MRI/FDG PET fusion in select pts.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: 2-year local control for **invasive and non-invasive** disease, metastasis-free survival, OS, bladder preservation and toxicity. Invasive recurrence analysed by Fine-Gray competing-risk models.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Invasive recurrence was the only endpoint that separated (**adjusted SHR 0.20, p=0.035**); non-invasive recurrence, metastasis and OS did not differ. Full arm values in the table.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G2+ GU 17.9% vs 22.1% and G2+ GI 5.1% vs 7.4% (escalated vs standard), **no difference** (p=0.8, p=0.9). G3 toxicity only in 2 standard-dose pts; no early cessation.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: BC2001 and BCON built modern TMT on radiosensitisation of whole-bladder RT, not on dose to the primary. RAIDER tested tumour-focused adaptive escalation prospectively; this series adds a routine-practice, CBCT-era hypofractionated experience in the same direction.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents unifocal, predominantly T2, M0 MIBC treated with curative hypofractionated TMT under daily CBCT. Does not represent multifocal disease, metastatic or palliative-intent pts.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Asymmetric outcome ascertainment**: 3 standard-arm recurrences were imaging-only and presumed invasive, while every escalated recurrence was cystoscopy-confirmed. Chemo use (56% vs 44%) and hypofractionation (97% vs 87%) also favoured the escalated cohort, and f/u starts at 3 mo, short for late bladder toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The in-field failure pattern in the standard cohort gives escalation a mechanistic rationale; the magnitude is not trustworthy given selection. Bladder preservation was high in both groups partly because relapsed pts were unfit for cystectomy, so it conflates control with fitness.

studies.interpretation:
The case for dose escalation in bladder preservation rests on a pattern-of-failure argument, and this series supplies that argument more convincingly than its headline hazard ratio. In the standard-dose cohort, invasive failures sat overwhelmingly at the original tumour site (14 within versus 2 outside), which is what you would expect if dose to the gross tumour, not field extent, is the limiting factor. Boosting the primary through a simultaneous integrated boost while holding the whole-bladder prescription at 55Gy/20fx or 64Gy/32fx is the logical response, and the escalated cohort recorded only 2 invasive recurrences, one of them inside the boost field. The direction is biologically coherent. The open question is how much of the magnitude survives the design.

Less than the SHR of 0.20 implies. Every escalated patient had unifocal disease, against 65% of the standard cohort, and hydronephrosis, a marker of deeper or bulkier tumour and an independent adverse factor for OS in this same dataset, was present in 10% versus 28%. Unifocal tumours without hydronephrosis are exactly where a boost is technically easy to plan and where local control would be better regardless of dose. A Fine-Gray model adjusting only for T stage, with 2 invasive events on one side, cannot separate dose from that selection, and an interval running from 0.05 to 0.89 shows how fragile the point estimate is. Ascertainment tilts the same way: three standard-arm recurrences were imaging-detected in pts unfit for cystoscopy and classified as presumed invasive, while every escalated recurrence was cystoscopy-confirmed. Frailer pts, worse tumours and softer outcome definitions all sat in the comparator arm.

Against the trials that define TMT practice, the relevance is specific rather than general. BC2001 and BCON built the modern approach on radiosensitisation of whole-bladder RT, and neither asked whether more dose to the primary helps. RAIDER approached that question prospectively with adaptive tumour-focused planning. This series belongs next to that work as routine-practice evidence that a primary boost is deliverable in hypofractionated schedules under daily CBCT, without an early toxicity price. That is a feasibility and hypothesis contribution, not an efficacy one.

Toxicity is the more reassuring part. G2+ GU and GI rates were not higher with escalation, and grade 3 events occurred only in the standard cohort. But a median follow-up of 23 months, with a range starting at 3, is short for contracture, haematuria and reduced capacity, which is where a boost would be expected to cost. Absence of an early signal is not absence of late harm.

The null metastasis and OS results should not be read as evidence against escalation. In a cohort where half did not receive chemotherapy because of poor PS, and where chemo omission and hydronephrosis dominated survival, a local-control gain in 107 pts would not be expected to reach OS. Bladder preservation was high in both groups partly because relapsed pts were too unfit for cystectomy, so that endpoint conflates control with fitness. What would make this result wrong is simple: if unifocal, non-hydronephrotic tumours do this well at standard dose. Only a randomised or carefully matched prospective comparison answers that, and this dataset is a reasonable justification for running one.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Standard-dose invasive failures clustered at the original tumour site (14 within vs 2 outside), the dose-limited failure pattern a primary boost targets. The SIB (up to 60Gy/20fx or 70Gy/32fx) on daily CBCT added no G2+ GU/GI toxicity at 23 mo median f/u, so the open question is late effects rather than deliverability.

open_questions: Does SIB primary-tumour escalation reduce invasive recurrence in a randomised TMT trial?
Is the benefit preserved in multifocal MIBC?
Late GU toxicity beyond 2 years with a 60Gy/20fx or 70Gy/32fx boost?

studies.name: Proactive immune cell sparing SBRT (NCT04273893)
studies.tldr: Immune-sparing lung SBRT planning cut ALC loss: overall improvement 13.4% (95% CI 2.8-24.0), G3 lymphopenia 0% vs 15.4%; survival trend unpowered.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase II, 1:1, stratified by tumor location (central vs peripheral), assignments not masked

details.text: 🔍 55 enrolled and randomized, 4 withdrew/ineligible → 25 optimized vs 26 standard analyzed

details: 🔍 Early-stage NSCLC, inoperable or declining surgery; recurrent NSCLC eligible; no systemic therapy within 1 yr before or 6 mo after SBRT

details.text: 💊 SBRT 45-60 Gy/5 fx via IMRT/VMAT, 6X-FFF; both arms met RTOG 0813/0915 dosimetric criteria

details: 🔍 Optimized arm added heart, great vessels, thoracic spine and lymph-node-stations as immune OARs

details.text: 📊 Model-estimated % ALC change from baseline (primary endpoint)
📊 Central tumors (n=15): overall ALC improvement 29.5% (95% CI 10.1-48.9), p=0.004

details: 📊 Peripheral PTV >20cc: 13.5%, p=0.124; peripheral PTV <20cc showed no difference
📊 G3 lymphopenia 15.4% standard vs 0% optimized (risk difference -15.4%, p=0.04)

details.text: 📐 Mean V5 reduction, optimized vs standard plans
📊 2-yr survival, unplanned exploratory analysis

details: 📊 LN-station V5 <35.4cc vs ≥35.4cc: 2-yr OS 91.8% vs 57.5%, p=0.02 (dosimetric stratification, not randomized)

details.text: 💊 G3 AEs 2 optimized vs 4 standard; G2 24% vs 35%; no G2+ pneumonitis in either arm

details: ⚠️ Arm imbalance: central 36.0% vs 23.1%, Tx-naive 64.0% vs 88.5%
⚠️ Tx-naive 2-yr OS given as 93.4% in Results, 94.1% in Discussion; internal inconsistency
⚠️ medRxiv preprint, not peer-reviewed

verdict.rationale: Preprint, small randomized phase II with unmasked lymphocyte surrogate primary; survival analyses unplanned and unpowered. Arm imbalance in central and treatment-naive pts.
verdict.audience: Early-stage NSCLC, inoperable or declining surgery, SBRT without systemic therapy

studies.significance: The dosimetric lever is low-dose spill, not the target: V5 to thoracic spine fell 87% and LN stations 58% with lung V5 down only 8%, all within RTOG 0813/0915 criteria. Benefit concentrated in central tumors (29.5% ALC gain) and was absent for peripheral PTV <20cc, so arc and beam-angle choices for central SBRT are where this plan change applies.
studies.monday_clinic: In a central early-stage NSCLC going to 5-fx SBRT without systemic therapy, this supports treating heart, great vessels, thoracic spine and LN stations as low-dose avoidance structures; it does not change planning for small peripheral PTVs under 20cc or establish a survival gain.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized phase II**, 1:1, stratified by tumor location, permuted blocks, **not masked**. Enrolled Feb 2020 to Apr 2023; 55 randomized, 51 analyzed (25 vs 26). Survival and subgroup analyses were **unplanned and exploratory**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Early-stage NSCLC (AJCC v8), ECOG 0-2, unable or unwilling to undergo surgery; recurrent NSCLC eligible. Excluded RT within 2 yr and **systemic therapy within 1 yr prior or 6 mo after**. Median age 74 both arms.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **45-60 Gy in 5 fx** (majority 60 Gy/5), IMRT or VMAT, 4DCT ITV plus 5mm radial / 8mm sup-inf PTV margin. Optimized plans met standard RTOG 0813/0915 criteria while minimizing dose to heart, great vessels, thoracic spine and lymph-node-stations, contoured to a 40 cGy/fx low-dose envelope.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** in vivo lymphocyte depletion at end of treatment, 4 wk and 6 mo; safety/toxicity (co-primary). Algorithm performance reported separately. OS and EFS descriptive only.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Central tumors drove the effect (**29.5%** overall ALC improvement, p=0.004); peripheral PTV <20cc showed no difference. **G3 lymphopenia 0% vs 15.4%** (p=0.04).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3 AEs 2 (lung infection) optimized vs 4 standard (dyspnea, hypoxia, lung infection); all recovered. **No G2+ pneumonitis** or G4+ events in either arm.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Both arms sat inside RTOG 0813/0915 planning criteria, so the comparison isolates immune-OAR avoidance on top of current SBRT constraints. Prior lymphopenia-outcome links in thoracic RT are largely associative; this is a randomized test that planning alone moves ALC.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents inoperable early-stage NSCLC treated with 5-fx SBRT alone, especially central tumors. Does not represent SBRT combined with immunotherapy or chemotherapy, conventionally fractionated chemoRT, or small peripheral PTVs under 20cc.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Arm imbalance** in central (36.0% vs 23.1%) and treatment-naive (64.0% vs 88.5%) pts biases the survival comparison. Tx-naive OS reported as 93.4% and 94.1% in different sections. LN V5 OS split is a non-randomized dosimetric stratification.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Establishes feasibility and an ALC effect, not a clinical one. Whether sparing lymphocytes during SBRT translates to EFS/OS, or to better IO response when combined, needs the multi-institutional powered trial the authors call for.

studies.interpretation:
The core claim here is narrow and, within the trial's own terms, reasonably well supported: when lung SBRT plans are built to push low dose away from the heart, great vessels, thoracic spine and mediastinal nodal stations, peripheral lymphocyte counts fall less. The primary endpoint was prespecified, randomization was stratified on the variable most likely to confound it (tumor location), and the direction held at every timepoint even as the 6-month difference lost significance. That is a cleaner answer than most of the lymphopenia literature in thoracic RT, which has largely been built on retrospective associations between dose to circulating blood and outcomes, where sicker pts with larger or more central tumors both receive more dose and do worse for reasons unrelated to lymphocytes.

What the trial does not settle is whether any of this matters clinically. ALC is a surrogate, and the step from a smaller ALC nadir to better tumor control has not been shown in a randomized setting. The survival analyses were unplanned, the trial was explicitly not powered for them, and the numbers invite over-reading. The treatment-naive subgroup shows the largest OS gap, but that subgroup is itself unbalanced between arms (64.0% vs 88.5% treatment-naive), and the manuscript quotes two different values for the optimized-arm OS in that group. The most striking survival split, 2-year OS 91.8% vs 57.5% by lymph-node-station V5 above or below 35.4cc, is a dosimetric stratification across both arms rather than a randomized comparison, and nodal-station V5 will track tumor centrality and size, both of which carry independent prognostic weight. A skeptic would say the survival data are hypothesis-generating at best and confounded at worst.

The more transferable finding for a planner is where the benefit lives. The effect concentrated in central tumors, was modest and non-significant for peripheral PTVs over 20cc, and was absent for small peripheral targets. That pattern is biologically coherent: a small peripheral lesion simply does not bathe much of the mediastinum or spine in low dose, so there is little to spare. It also means the intervention costs almost nothing where it does not help, since lung low-dose volume barely changed and toxicity did not rise. For central SBRT, where the dose bath through the heart and great vessels is unavoidable to some degree, treating those structures as low-dose avoidance volumes is a planning choice that stays inside RTOG 0813/0915 criteria.

The open-label design matters less than usual because the primary endpoint is a lab value, but it would matter for any subjective secondary. The preprint status also matters: peer review may tighten the internal inconsistencies and clarify how the 40 cGy/fx nodal-station envelope was contoured, which is the step most likely to vary between centers.

The most interesting forward question is the combination one. The exclusion of systemic therapy makes this a clean SBRT-alone population, but the rationale for sparing lymphocytes is strongest when SBRT is paired with checkpoint inhibition, where effector T cells are the mechanism. This trial cannot speak to that setting. For now it supports immune-OAR-aware planning as a low-cost refinement for central early-stage NSCLC, and it frames, rather than answers, whether lymphocyte sparing changes outcomes.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The lever is low-dose spill, not target coverage: thoracic spine V5 fell 87% and LN-station V5 58% with lung V5 down only 8%, inside RTOG 0813/0915 criteria. Gains concentrated in central tumors (29.5% ALC improvement) and vanished for peripheral PTV <20cc, so beam and arc choices for central SBRT are where this applies.

open_questions: Does lymphocyte-sparing SBRT improve EFS or OS in a powered trial?
Does immune-sparing planning enhance SBRT plus immunotherapy outcomes?
Optimal dose limits for thoracic spine and lymph-node-stations

papers.title: First Measurement: Proactive Immune Cell Sparing in Radiation Therapy
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose Radiation Therapy (RT) can modulate the immune system and generate anti-tumor T cells. However, this anti-tumor-activity is countered by radiation-induced immunosuppression (RIIS). Clinical advantages of proactively sparing RT dose to immune rich organs have not previously been evaluated. Methods We conducted a phase II randomized trial from 2020 to 2023, enrolling 51 early-stage lung cancer patients treated with SBRT, to evaluate the effect of dose reduction to immune rich organs on RIIS. Two groups were: RIIS-optimized-treatment (lowering the dose to blood, bone-marrow and lymph-node-stations) and standard-treatment. All treatments followed national protocol guidelines. Peripheral blood was collected at baseline, immediately, 4-weeks and 6-months post-treatment. Results ALC changes from baseline immediately, 4-weeks and 6-months post-SBRT are: optimized-arm: -16%, -22%, -16%, standard-arm: -31%, -34%, -26%, leading to an overall-all-time-point improvement in ALC reduction in the optimized-arm compared to the standard-arm of 13.4 (5.3) % (95% CI, 2.8 to 24.0; p = 0.01). Central tumors had the largest improvement in ALC from baseline: optimized-arm: - 8%, -18%, -14%, standard-arm: -39%, -43%, -47%, leading to an overall-all-time-point improvement in ALC reduction in the optimized-arm compared to the standard-arm of 29.5 (9.6) % (95% CI, 10.1 to 48.9; p = 0.004). Grade 3 lymphopenia occurred in 15.4% of standard arm patients but was absent in the optimized arm. Additionally, 2.8 times more patients in the optimized arm experienced an ALC increase post-SBRT. Dose to organs such as the heart, great vessels, thoracic spine, and lymph nodes significantly correlated with RIIS. A trend towards increased Event-Free-Survival (two-year: 75.0% (SE = 10.8%) versus 59.8% (SE = 11.2%), p =0·10) and Overall Survival (two-year: 93.4% (SE=6.1%) versus 69.4% (SE=10.5%), p =0·14) was observed with optimized-planning compared to standard-planning in treatment naïve patients. Conclusion Reducing RT dose to immune rich organs significantly reduces RIIS compared to standard-of-care. This has implications in enhancing immune system mediated anti-tumor-activity. (Funded by National Cancer Institute and others. ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04273893 )
